# Muttātherīgāthā (Thig 1.11)

**ID:** Thig 1.11

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Muttātherīgāthā* (Thig 1.11) is a short poetic utterance preserved in the *Therīgāthā* of the Khuddaka Nikāya, attributed to the senior nun (therī) Muttā [SuttaCentral; Young 2004]. In the verse, Muttā celebrates her release through an extended wordplay on her name (*mutta*, meaning "freed" or "liberated"), exclaiming that she is well freed from three crooked things: the mortar, the pestle, and her crooked or hunchbacked husband [Young 2004; Blackstone 2000]. She declares that she is simultaneously liberated from the cycle of rebirth and death, having rooted out the craving that leads to renewed existence (*bhavanetta*) [Powers 2016; Young 2004]. The traditional background narrative preserved in Dhammapāla's commentary explains that Muttā was the daughter of an impoverished brahmin married to a hunchbacked man, who agreed to release her from marriage so she could renounce domestic life [Powers 2016].

Scholars have noted that Muttā's poem serves as a classic expression of female liberation in early Buddhist monasticism, highlighting the rejection of marital burdens and domestic drudgery alongside spiritual realization [Young 2004; Leeming 2014]. Kathryn R. Blackstone compares Muttā's poem with a closely parallel verse spoken by the monk Sumaṅgala in the *Theragāthā*, who employs an identical syntactic structure to celebrate release from three crooked agricultural implements (sickles, plows, and spades) [Blackstone 2000]. Whereas Sumaṅgala celebrates freedom from secular agricultural labor, Muttā distinctively emphasizes liberation from her marital relationship and domestic responsibilities [Blackstone 2000].

No direct early parallels for this verse are preserved in Chinese Āgama, Sanskrit, or Tibetan corpora [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Automated text-reuse analysis via DharmaNexus confirms four matches within Pali literature, all with Dhammapāla's commentary, the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā* (matching segments 0.3–2.1 with 96% similarity), where the verse is embedded and commented upon [DharmaNexus]. The text has been translated into multiple modern languages, including English translations by Bhikkhu Sujato and Ayya Soma listed on SuttaCentral [SuttaCentral].
